transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-26
Time: 15:00 PDT (22:00Z)
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Fenrir - Head of ML), Priya Nair (Fenrir - Platform Eng), Ethan Cho (Fenrir - CTO)

Summary (auto):
Fenrir Payments evaluating Redwood for production inference. Primary focus on latency & throughput: p95 latency targets for chat streaming, concurrency needs (200+ concurrent users), token/sec throughput for batch scoring, and dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs. Security questions: SOC2, KMS, VPC. Action items: pricing + SOC2 docs, benchmark script, sample prompts.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — i'm Maya from Redwood, i'm the AE on this account, with me is Liam our solutions engineer. How are you all?
[00:09] Diego: Good, thanks. Diego here. We'll try to keep this focused, we have a hard latency SLO we need to meet.
[00:13] Priya: Hi all, Priya - i'll cover infra / networking questions.
[00:16] Ethan: Ethan here. I'm mainly listening but will chime on ops / cost.
[00:20] Liam: Great. Quick agenda — understand current stack and targets, talk about hosted vs dedicated vs private for your use case, dig into p95 and concurrency numbers, and propose next steps including a bench. Sound okay?
[00:30] Diego: Yep. Our app is a realtime payments auth assistant — low latency is critical. We want p95 generation latency under 350ms for single-turn streaming replies at ~256 tokens average, and under 200ms for embeddings. Concurrency: baseline 200 concurrent active users during peak, spikes to 700 for short windows.
[00:52] Maya: Okay that's helpful. Are those p95 targets end-to-end from app to final token delivered or just model-side?
[01:00] Diego: That's end-to-end from our API to response. Our network adds roughly 50–80ms depending on region. So model-side should be around 200–250ms p95 for generation.
[01:12] Liam: Cool — what's your current model and deployment? Open models or a hosted provider?
[01:18] Diego: We currently run a trimmed open model on self-hosted infra for early tests but it's noisy. We're evaluating Redwood hosted first, but open to dedicated pool or private VPC deployment if we need consistent SLOs and data controls.
[01:33] Priya: Also want to understand egress costs and whether we can do VPC peering or private link.
[01:38] Liam: Understood. For p95 generation at 256 tokens, with streaming, there are a few levers: model variant (smaller vs larger), quantization, batching, and KV cache for repeated prefixes. Redwood Dedicated gives predictable GPU pools, which helps hitting p95 at scale. Hosted has autoscaling but bursts can add variance.
[01:56] Diego: What's your baseline tokens/sec for a single stream on a A100-like GPU?
[02:01] Liam: For a typical 7B-13B quantized model on an A100 or H100, you might see ~150–400 tokens/sec single-stream depending on attention patterns and optimizations; latency per token is small but end-to-end includes kernel setup and decoder loops. With Redwood's runtime optimizations and continuous batching disabled for strict latency SLOs, you can get lower variance.
[02:25] Maya: Important to call out that streaming behavior matters — if you need first token within X ms vs completion p95, that changes recommendations.
[02:33] Diego: We care about time-to-first-byte (TTFB) primarily; streaming start within 120ms would be ideal, full response p95 within 350ms.
[02:42] Liam: That's tight but achievable for many prompt shapes with smaller models and dedicated nodes. If you need context windows >1k tokens it changes the compute cost.
[02:52] Priya: Our average prompt length is 120 tokens, completion ~130 tokens. We also use user history caching frequently.
[02:59] Liam: Okay so average sequence length lower than 256 helps. Caching repeated prefixes with KV will shave off a chunk of latency for returning users.
[03:08] Ethan: For concurrency — 200 concurrent active streams, are we talking active decoding concurrency (i.e., tokens being generated simultaneously) or number of web-socket connections?
[03:18] Diego: Active decoding concurrency. Connections might be 3x that but only a fraction are actively decoding at once.
[03:24] Liam: Good distinction. For active decoding concurrency 200, we typically recommend either Dedicated with reserved GPUs sized for your p95 target or Hosted with a combination of burst capacity and fallback to smaller models during overload.
[03:37] Maya: Cost note: Dedicated gives predictable RU (reservation units) cost; Hosted is pay-as-you-go but potentially cheaper for smaller sustained loads.
[03:45] Diego: Can Redwood do auto-fallback? Like if we hit capacity, fallback to a quantized 7B for degraded quality but preserved latency?
[03:53] Liam: Yes — smart routing / automatic fallback to compatible model variants is part of the platform. You can set policy per-route to fallback and we capture metrics so you can measure quality deltas.
[04:04] Priya: On the networking side — what are options for private connectivity?
[04:08] Maya: For Private we offer VPC peering or private link and optional on-prem package. For Dedicated we also support customer VPC peering. Key management hooks (KMS/HSM) are available for Private and Dedicated.
[04:20] Priya: Good. We'll need to see network diagrams and our security team will want SOC2 docs.
[04:25] Maya: We'll share SOC2 and compliance kit after the call.
[04:28] Diego: How do you benchmark p95 at scale? What do you need from us to run a meaningful test?
[04:34] Liam: We usually ask for a representative prompt set (top-20 templates), token-length distribution, concurrency profile (active decoding conc), and a sample of streaming parameters (chunk size, flush interval). We'll provide a benchmark script that spins clients at target concurrency and measures p50/p95/p99 for time-to-first-byte and end-to-end completion.
[04:53] Diego: Any chance to run token/sec microbenchmarks vs. our current infra? We'd like relative numbers.
[04:58] Liam: Absolutely — we can run microbenchmarks (single-stream tokens/sec) and production-like scenarios. For real comparison we ask you to run the same script on your infra or we can replicate a snapshot of traffic to replicate a snapshot to Redwood test harness.
[05:14] Ethan: What's the turnaround time for a benchmark?
[05:16] Liam: If you provide prompts and traffic profile within a few days, we can run an initial dedicated-hosted comparison in 3–5 business days. A full dedicated cluster run takes longer if we need to provision reserved capacity.
[05:27] Priya: About encryption at rest and in transit — we need KMS integration and audit logs for tokens. How granular are your audit logs?
[05:36] Maya: We provide request/response tracing (token-level cost breakdowns and latency traces) for Redwood Console. Audit logs include who accessed keys and admin actions; for Private deployments we can route logs to your SIEM.
[05:46] Diego: Are there cases where Hosted just can't hit p95 targets due to noisy neighbors?
[05:51] Liam: Hosted uses multi-tenant pools which can introduce some variance at peak; Dedicated solves that by giving you reserved GPUs. For extremely tight p95 SLOs with bursts to 700 concurrent active decodes, Dedicated or Private is safer. We also support burst capacity attachments to Dedicated for short windows.
[06:08] Diego: If we go Dedicated, what's the typical GPU fleet? A100 vs H100?
[06:13] Liam: We support both; H100 has better throughput for larger models and better quantization support for certain kernels. The right choice depends on model size and your latency target.
[06:22] Priya: We plan to use a quantized 13B variant for now — any rough numbers on expected p95 for 120+130 token sequences on H100?
[06:32] Liam: Ballpark: for a well-optimized 13B quantized model on H100, time-to-first-byte might be in the 80–160ms range and end-to-end for 250 tokens could be 180–300ms p95, but we need your prompt shapes and beam settings to be precise.
[06:49] Diego: That aligns with what we hoped. Can Redwood run tests that measure time-to-first-token vs per-token latency?
[06:56] Liam: Yes — our benchmark script measures TTFB, per-token throughput, and tail latency. We'll also expose the KV cache hit rates if you use caching.
[07:06] Maya: Another operational thing — do you want streaming chunk sizes tuned? Many customers see better TTFB by lowering chunk batch sizes at the cost of throughput.
[07:15] Diego: We're willing to trade some throughput for lower TTFB. Our user experience suffers if the first bytes are delayed.
[07:20] Liam: Ok we'll include a few variants: aggressive low-latency streaming config, balanced config, and high-throughput config for the bench.
[07:28] Priya: For the bench, will you need VPC peering to run on Private or can we stage data in a test VPC?
[07:34] Liam: For a Private run we need network setup; for hosted/dedicated we can run from our test harness without peering. If you want to simulate your network latency we can inject RTT to emulate your region.
[07:45] Ethan: Cost question — what's the marginal cost per 1k tokens for Dedicated vs Hosted?
[07:51] Maya: Pricing is nuanced: Hosted is pay-as-you-go per-token; Dedicated is a monthly reservation plus lower per-token execution costs. We'll send a pricing example for your concurrency and token volumes in the deck.
[08:02] Diego: Security — do you support SSO/SAML and RBAC?
[08:06] Maya: Yes, both SSO with SAML and granular RBAC. For Private we can integrate with your IdP directly.
[08:12] Priya: Any limitations for streaming with encryption and private links?
[08:16] Liam: No — we support TLS in transit, and private link peering doesn't affect streaming semantics.
[08:21] Diego: Ok, let's outline the bench plan and what we need: top-20 prompts, token distribution, concurrency profile, and a staging API key?
[08:30] Liam: Correct. Also, please indicate any disallowed data that we should strip from logs for the bench run.
[08:36] Diego: We'll redact PCI-like tokens; bench will use synthetic numbers.
[08:40] Maya: Great. Any other blockers?
[08:43] Ethan: Only one — we need to involve procurement if we move to Dedicated. Otherwise procurement won't sign without SLA numbers.
[08:50] Maya: We can include SLA language in the pricing pack and propose a pilot with an SLA for the initial month.
[08:56] Priya: Timeline — if we get the bench script Friday, we can run a basic run next week.
[09:02] Liam: Sounds good. We'll prepare three configs and send the script.
[09:07] Diego: One more technical — how do you measure and report model regressions during rollout? We need a way to detect quality drops when you fallback or upgrade model versions.
[09:16] Liam: Redwood Optimize ties model quality monitoring to prompt sets/evals. We can run canary sets and regression alerts for top N prompts, with configurable thresholds.
[09:26] Diego: Perfect.
[09:28] Maya: Recap / next steps — Maya to send pricing + SOC2 + network diagrams; Liam to send benchmark script (three configs) and instructions; Fenrir to provide prompt set and token distribution; schedule bench early next week. Anything to add?
[09:43] Diego: Nope that's it. Thanks.
[09:45] Priya: Thanks all.
[09:47] Ethan: Thanks.
[09:48] Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up via email with the items discussed.

End of meeting.
